sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
Welcome. Today we meet one of the most important people in the entire Bible: Abraham. Three of the world's great religions look back to him, and the New Testament calls him the father of all who believe. Yet when we first meet him, he is simply a man named Abram, living with his family, with no children and no idea of the adventure ahead.

His story is told in Genesis chapters twelve through twenty-two. It is a story about faith — what it is, how it grows, and how it is tested. As you listen, ask yourself: what does it mean to really trust God's promises, especially when you have to wait?

sections.title: The Story, Part 1
sections.text:
The story begins with a call. Genesis chapter twelve, verses one and two: “Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee: And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing.”

Think about what God was asking. Leave your homeland. Leave your relatives. Leave your father's house. And go — where? God didn't give him a map. He simply said, to a land that I will show you. The book of Hebrews puts it this way: “he went out, not knowing whither he went.”

And Abram went. He took his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, and everything they owned, and they traveled to the land of Canaan. There God appeared to him and said, “Unto thy seed will I give this land.” Abram built an altar there and worshiped the Lord.

But there was a problem with the promise. A great nation needs children, and Abram and Sarai had none. Sarai was barren, and they were both getting older. Years went by.

One night God brought Abram outside and said, “Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them.” Then He said, “So shall thy seed be.” Abram looked up at that sky full of stars. Nothing had changed in his circumstances. He was still old, and Sarai was still childless. But Genesis chapter fifteen, verse six tells us what happened in his heart: “And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.”

sections.title: The Story, Part 2
sections.text:
Abram's faith was real, but it wasn't perfect. At one point, tired of waiting, Abram and Sarai tried to make the promise happen their own way, and Abram had a son named Ishmael with Sarai's servant Hagar. It caused heartache for everyone. God was patient, but He made it clear that the promised son would come from Sarah.

When Abram was ninety-nine years old, God appeared to him again and changed his name. “Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham; for a father of many nations have I made thee.” God changed Sarai's name to Sarah as well. And He promised that Sarah would have a son within the year. Sarah laughed when she heard it — it sounded impossible. But the Lord asked, “Is any thing too hard for the LORD?”

And God did exactly what He said. Genesis chapter twenty-one, verse five: “And Abraham was an hundred years old, when his son Isaac was born unto him.” The name Isaac means laughter. Sarah said that God had made her laugh — this time with joy.

Then came the hardest moment of Abraham's life. God told him to take Isaac, his only son whom he loved, to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering. We can hardly imagine how Abraham felt. But early the next morning, he rose and went. As they climbed the mountain, Isaac carried the wood and asked, “Behold the fire and the wood: but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?” Abraham answered with words of deep faith: “My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering.”

At the top of the mountain, Abraham built the altar, laid the wood in order, and bound Isaac. But as he raised his hand, the angel of the Lord called to him from heaven and told him to stop. “Now I know that thou fearest God,” the angel said. Abraham looked up and saw a ram caught in a thicket by its horns. He offered the ram instead of his son. And Abraham called the name of that place Jehovah-jireh, which means, the Lord will provide.

sections.title: The Lesson
sections.text:
What does Abraham's life teach us?

First, faith often means taking a step before you can see the whole path. Abraham left home without knowing where he was going. Sometimes God shows us only the next step. Faith is taking it.

Second, faith means trusting God's timing. Abraham waited about twenty-five years for Isaac. When he tried to rush God's plan, it caused pain. Waiting is hard, but God's promises are never late.

Third, God counts faith as righteousness. Abraham wasn't made right with God by being perfect — he wasn't. He was made right with God by believing God. That is still how it works today. We are made right with God by trusting Him, and especially by trusting in Jesus.

And finally, God provides. On that mountain, God provided a ram in place of Isaac. Centuries later, on a hill not far from there, God provided His own Son, Jesus, as the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world. What God asked Abraham to give, God Himself gave for us.

sections.title: Prayer and Reflection
sections.text:
Think about a promise of God you are waiting on, or a step of faith you feel God may be asking you to take. What would it look like to trust Him with it today?

Let's pray. Father, thank You that You are faithful to every promise You make. When I can't see the whole path, help me take the next step. When I have to wait, help me trust Your timing. Thank You for providing the Lamb, Jesus, for me. In His name, Amen.

Thank you for listening. Next time, we'll hear the story of Joseph, a young man whose dreams took him on an unexpected journey.
